title: Why PED matters to sellers and government

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Explain what PED means for decision making by producers, consumers and government, and weigh how far a decision may safely lean on an elasticity figure.

blocks.heading: What each decision-maker does with the figure
blocks.text: A producer setting a price is likely to weigh PED, because the effect of a price change on its revenue depends on whether demand for its product is elastic or inelastic: with inelastic demand a rise tends to bring more revenue, with elastic demand the same rise tends to shrink it. That is why the Ruacana operator could raise its fare and collect more, while the juice stall in Opuwo lost N$200 by trying. A government choosing an indirect tax is likely to weigh PED for the same reason: a tax tends to raise more revenue where demand is price-inelastic, because quantity demanded falls little when the tax pushes the price up. Where a government wants a tax to change behaviour rather than raise money, it is likely to pick goods whose demand is price-elastic, because the quantity bought responds to the price rise the tax causes. Consumers read the figure from the other side, as the next section shows.

blocks.heading: What PED means for consumers
blocks.text:
Consumers use PED too, even without calculating it. Where demand for a good is price-inelastic - water, electricity, bus fares to work, basic medicines - a price rise leaves households little room to escape: they keep buying close to the same quantity, so they spend more on the good and have less left for everything else. A household in Katutura spending N$600 a month on electricity pays about N$720 if the price rises by 20 per cent and its use hardly changes, and the extra N$120 has to come out of food, clothing or saving. The squeeze tends to be hardest on low-income households, for whom such necessities take a larger share of income.

Where demand is price-elastic, as for soft drinks or one brand of cereal, consumers protect their budgets by switching to substitutes or going without, which is also why sellers of such goods hesitate to raise prices. PED shapes who pays an indirect tax as well: the more inelastic the demand for a good, the more of the tax tends to be passed on to consumers through a higher price, because they keep buying, while consumers of goods with elastic demand avoid much of it by switching. A household planning its budget can therefore expect price rises on necessities to bite, and can look for substitutes where they exist. Shoppers in the United Kingdom showed both responses when energy and food prices rose sharply in 2022: they paid the higher energy bills they could not avoid, and switched to cheaper own-brand groceries where they could.

blocks.heading: How far the figure can be trusted
blocks.text: PED is usually estimated from past market data, so decisions that lean on it carry the risk that the elasticity measured yesterday drifts as substitutes, incomes and tastes change: the Ruacana operator's 0.16 says little about a year in which a new road brings a bus service to the falls. A seller that raises price on the strength of an inelastic figure may find the estimate was taken before buyers adjusted, and the time determinant means responsiveness tends to grow as buyers find their alternatives.

blocks.heading: The one sentence to carry into the exam
blocks.text: PED measures how strongly buyers respond to a price change; the determinants say why the response is that size; the spending rules say what the response does to revenue; and producers and governments act on the number, at the risk that it was measured in a market that has since moved.
